subject: Convergence considerations with a shifted lognormal hierarchical model

messages.author: 0d4085b4474fa32a
messages.subject: Convergence considerations with a shifted lognormal hierarchical model
parts:
Hi, I'm back with my shifted-lognormal hierarchical model (this is my previous post), I
started to increase the complexity of the model, and I started to notice
problems in convergence. So I simplified everything again to check it.
Basically I'm trying to fit a model where reading times (rt) are assumed to be
produced by a shifted lognormal distribution. I'm assuming a general shift, a 
by-subject adjustment coming from a normal distribution centered in 0, an
intercept for the lognormal part (alpha), a fixed effect (beta), and 
by-subjects random intercept and slopes centered in 0 that they are somewhat
correlated: (the complete code is in shifted_log_simple.stan)


 transformed parameters{
 (...)
 for (i in 1:N_obs){
    mu[i] <- alpha  + x_betas[i] * beta +  
          x_u[i] * u[subj[i]];
    psi[i] <-  shift + shift_u[subj[i]]; //
  }
}


model {
 (...)
     (rt - psi) ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);
}



So the same parameters that don't get an Rhat of 1 in the complex mode, here
they are around 1.01-1.02 (while the other params are more in the
1.00something).

These parameters are the ones that are in a different scale than the rest:
alpha (the intercept of fixed effects) has an estimate around 5 (I simulate
this but that's also the case in "real life"), the intercept for shift is
around 200, while the adjustment for shift for participants is between 0-200.
(The other parameters are below 1). I checked the get_sampler_params, and I
noticed that Max treedepth reaches 11 and n_divergent has a Max of 1, which I
understand from the manual is something bad.

So from reading previous answers in the forum, I understand that there are two
possibilities: either to decrease the stepsize and increase the treedepth; or
to normalize the parameters to be near 1. I'm trying to avoid the first
possibility just because it's extremely slow. 

Regarding the second option, one problem that I face is that the
initialization fails unless I set init=0.

I'm normalizing the intercept alpha with alpha_k= mean(log(rt)), which is
always a bit bigger than the intercept, and the shifts with shift_k which is
mean(rt) also bigger than the shift. I'm doing this (in shifted_log_simple_norm.stan):

 for (i in 1:N_obs){
    mu[i] <- alpha * alpha_k + x_betas[i] * beta +  
          x_u[i] * u[subj[i]];
    psi[i] <-  shift_k * (shift + shift_u[subj[i]]); //
  }



First of all, it doesn't improve the Rhats (in fact all Rhats are
even bigger). So does it even make sense? (And I guess that constraining the
init to 0 is not ideal, but maybe a side effect of the problems I'm having).
And I still have the same problems with treedepth n_divergent. So my question
is: Is there a solution besides changing step size and the maximum tree depth?

I'm attaching my models to generate the data, to fit it in two different ways, r code and output.
Thanks 
Bruno

for constraints matching support.

It's an issue of parameterizing the model in a more friendly way. The
problem with all these hierarchical models is only a week identifiability
in play, especially if the hierarchical variance is high. You can check out
the pairs plot of the posterior to see if any correlations jump out at you (just
be warned it won't work for more than 10 or so input variables at a time).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Convergence considerations with a shifted lognormal hierarchical model
parts:
For understanding HMC, start with Radford Neal's paper in the MCMC
Handbook (it's a free sample chapter online). Then maybe go to
something like Michael's paper on hierarchical modeling on arXiv.

But the issue isn't HMC or Gibbs or Metropolis per se, but the interaction
of those algorithms and step sizes with floating point arithmetic.

The point is that you want to figure out where you get overflow
or underflow in the exploration of the posterior. This often happens when
parameters get pushed near boundaries. Parameters constrained to be in (0, 1)
can underflow to 0 or overflow to 1, for example.

You could do worse than reading the Wikipedia:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_point

Beyond that, I wouldn't mind getting a good recommendation for
a numerical analysis book myself.

It'll also be a problem if your model's not identified. You could start
with the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

- Bob

Michael has a bunch of papers about HMC but I think this is the one Bob was suggesting. Some of the other papers are much more challenging reads (not that this one is easy) so this is probably a good one to start with after reading Radford's book chapter.
